---
title: "Selection sort — a formal proof of correctness"
---

Written to be worked at the board. It leans on two results rather than
reproving them: `idxOfMin`, proved in lecture 4/5, and `swap`, assumed.

## The code

```cpp
void selectionSort (vector<int>& C) {
    for (int i = 0; i < C.size(); i++) {
        int m = idxOfMin(C, i);
        swap(C, m, i);
    }
}
```

Write $n$ for `C.size()`, and $C_0$ for the contents of `C` on entry. Note $n$
does not change: nothing in the loop resizes `C`.

## What we are allowed to assume

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
**Lemma 1 (`idxOfMin`).** For $0 \le a < n$, `idxOfMin(C, a)` returns an index
$\ell$ with $a \le \ell < n$ and
$$C[\ell] \;=\; \min_{a \le j < n} C[j],$$
and does not modify `C`.
:::

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
**Lemma 2 (`swap`).** `swap(C, p, q)` leaves `C` with $C'[p] = C[q]$,
$C'[q] = C[p]$, and $C'[k] = C[k]$ for every $k \notin \{p, q\}$. In
particular it is a transposition, so it permutes the contents of `C`.
:::

## What we are proving

::: {.callout-important appearance="minimal"}
**Theorem.** After `selectionSort(C)` returns, `C` is a permutation of $C_0$
and $C[0] \le C[1] \le \cdots \le C[n-1]$.
:::

Both halves are needed. Sortedness alone is satisfied by a function that
overwrites the array with zeroes.

## The invariant

At the top of iteration $i$ — meaning just before the guard is tested with the
loop variable equal to $i$ — for $0 \le i \le n$:

::: {.callout-tip appearance="minimal"}
**$P(i)$:**

(a) `C` is a permutation of $C_0$;
(b) $C[0] \le C[1] \le \cdots \le C[i-1]$;
(c) $\displaystyle\max_{0 \le k < i} C[k] \;\le\; \min_{i \le j < n} C[j]$.
:::

Clauses (b) and (c) are vacuous when $i = 0$; (c) is also vacuous when $i = n$.

Clause (c) is the one that does not appear in the theorem. It is carried purely
to make the induction go through — see the remark at the end.

## a) Initialization

Take $i = 0$.

(a) No statement has executed, so `C` holds $C_0$, and the identity is a
permutation.

(b) The range $C[0..{-1}]$ is empty, and the empty sequence is sorted.

(c) There is no $k$ with $0 \le k < 0$, so the maximum is over an empty set and
the claim is vacuous.

Hence $P(0)$. $\qquad\blacksquare$

## b) Restoration

Assume $P(i)$ holds at the top of iteration $i$, and that the guard passed, so
$i < n$. Let `C` denote the contents at the top of the iteration and $C'$ the
contents after the body runs. We show $P(i+1)$ holds of $C'$.

The body does two things:

$$m \;=\; \texttt{idxOfMin(C, i)}, \qquad \texttt{swap(C, m, i)}.$$

By Lemma 1, $i \le m < n$ and
$$C[m] \;=\; \min_{i \le j < n} C[j], \tag{$\star$}$$
and `C` is unchanged by the call. By Lemma 2,
$$C'[i] = C[m], \qquad C'[m] = C[i], \qquad C'[k] = C[k] \text{ otherwise.}$$

**(a) Permutation.** `idxOfMin` does not modify `C`, and `swap` is a
transposition. A composition of permutations is a permutation, so by the
inductive hypothesis $C'$ is a permutation of $C_0$.

**(b) The prefix is sorted.** We must show
$C'[0] \le \cdots \le C'[i]$.

Since $m \ge i$, the swap touches only indices $\ge i$, so
$$C'[k] = C[k] \quad \text{for all } k < i,$$
and by the inductive hypothesis (b) this prefix is sorted. It remains to check
the join, that $C'[i-1] \le C'[i]$, and only when $i \ge 1$.

By the inductive hypothesis (c),
$$C[i-1] \;\le\; \max_{0 \le k < i} C[k] \;\le\; \min_{i \le j < n} C[j]
\;\overset{(\star)}{=}\; C[m] \;=\; C'[i],$$
and $C'[i-1] = C[i-1]$, so $C'[i-1] \le C'[i]$ as required.

When $i = 0$ the range $C'[0..0]$ is a single element and is sorted trivially.

**(c) The prefix stays below the suffix.** We must show
$$\max_{0 \le k < i+1} C'[k] \;\le\; \min_{i+1 \le j < n} C'[j].$$

By part (b) just proved, $C'[0..i]$ is sorted, so its maximum is its last
entry:
$$\max_{0 \le k \le i} C'[k] \;=\; C'[i] \;=\; C[m].$$

For the right-hand side, compare the two suffixes as multisets. The swap moves
$C[m]$ to position $i$ and $C[i]$ to position $m$, and both $i$ and $m$ lie in
$[i, n)$, so
$$\{\, C'[j] : i+1 \le j < n \,\} \;=\; \{\, C[j] : i \le j < n \,\} \setminus \{ C[m] \}.$$

Every element of $\{C[j] : i \le j < n\}$ is $\ge C[m]$ by $(\star)$, since
$C[m]$ is the minimum of exactly that set. Removing one element cannot
introduce anything smaller, so every remaining element is $\ge C[m] = C'[i]$,
which is the claim.

Hence $P(i+1)$. $\qquad\blacksquare$

## c) Termination

The loop variable starts at $0$, increases by exactly $1$ per iteration, and is
tested against the fixed bound $n$. So after $n$ iterations the guard fails and
control leaves the loop with $i = n$.

$P(n)$ therefore holds, and reading it off:

- (a) `C` is a permutation of $C_0$;
- (b) $C[0] \le C[1] \le \cdots \le C[n-1]$ — the whole array is sorted;
- (c) vacuous.

Together, (a) and (b) are exactly the theorem. $\qquad\blacksquare$

## Remark: why clause (c) is there

Drop (c) and the proof fails at one specific line. In part (b) we needed
$C'[i-1] \le C'[i]$, and the only thing that delivers it is knowing that
everything already placed is no larger than anything still to come. Sortedness
of the prefix alone says nothing about how the prefix compares to the rest, so
the newly placed element could land below its predecessor.

So (c) is not part of what we set out to prove, and it is not used at
termination — it retires there, vacuous. It exists solely so that the inductive
step can be taken. That is strengthening the induction hypothesis: the
statement you can prove is sometimes stronger than the one you want.

## Remark: the last iteration

The loop runs to $i = n-1$, where `idxOfMin(C, n-1)` must return $n-1$ and the
swap exchanges an element with itself. It is harmless, and the proof covers it
without a special case, but the loop could equally run to $n-2$. Worth a
sentence if someone asks — it is the same observation as the final pass of a
bubble sort doing nothing.
